column4: Moses begins by asking “اشرح لي صدري”; the source-section root sh-r-ḥ links this opening of the chest to the section’s first expansion, while his petition makes the receiving of expanded capacity explicit.
Moses immediately asks “ويسر لي أمري” after the chest-opening request; the sequence joins expanded capacity to an eased task, a pairing the section develops before the burden is lifted.

Moses asks for a “وزير” from his family; the source-section root w-z-r names the bearer behind 94’s word for burden, so this passage stages the helper that the section says its own speaker does not need.
20:29 requests a family vizier, and this next ayah names Harun as that helper; the name completes the human-support scene that contrasts with the burden removed directly in the section.

The source section explicitly gives the secondary gloss of w-z-r as “shelter”; 75:11 says “لَا وَزَرَ,” no refuge, carrying that sense into the Judgment scene and clarifying why the section ends by turning to God.

75:11 denies refuge and 75:12 supplies “إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ”; the latter’s own contribution is the turn toward the Lord, matching the section’s final words and identifying the destination after refuge fails.
The people who deny the meeting are described as carrying “أوزارهم على ظهورهم”; the source-section root w-z-r and its load-on-the-back image become an explicit scene of burdens carried on backs.

In describing the Messenger’s followers, this ayah says he removes “إصرهم والأغلال” from them; that unloading of burden and shackles parallels the section’s load taken off the back and makes relief concrete.

This ayah introduces ships and livestock as mounts; 43:13 completes the scene by settling on their backs and remembering God, while 43:14 gives the riders’ return to their Lord. This row supplies the rideable creatures.
The riders settle “على ظهورها” and then remember their Lord’s blessing; this is the section’s specific mount-back, back-to-remembrance sequence, with riding joined to gratitude.
The riding scene ends with “إلى ربنا لمنقلبون”; this ayah contributes the riders’ stated return to their Lord, which echoes the section’s final “إلى ربك.”
God’s animals carry heavy loads to distant lands that people could not reach without hardship; this supplies a literal burden-bearing transport scene alongside the section’s back and mount imagery.

16:7 describes animals carrying heavy loads, and this next ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys for riding and adornment; its own contribution is the range of mounts behind the section’s riding image.
The mother is said to have carried her child “وهنا على وهن”; this makes bodily carrying a child through successive weakness a direct counterpart to the section’s pregnancy-as-weight image.
This ayah says a mother carried and gave birth to her child with hardship; its paired carrying and delivery stages correspond to the section’s birth scene and sharpen the weight’s release at birth.
The mother’s carrying and delivery “كرها” supply a second direct formulation of childbirth under strain, the birth-weight image that the section places beside debt and riding.
The waiting period for a pregnant woman ends when she delivers, and the ayah promises that God makes the affair easy for the God-conscious; it joins childbirth’s carried term to ease.

This passage forbids harming a divorced mother to constrain her and speaks of nursing for payment and consultation; it gives the breastfeeding difficulty that the section names as another burden-bearing scene.
The debtor in hardship must be given respite until ease, and remission is praised; this is the section’s debt scene, where the due weight is allowed to remain until the debtor can bear it.

The source section sets 94’s “with hardship” beside this ayah’s “بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا” (ease after hardship); its own contribution is a real after-then-ease formulation that makes the section’s “with” relation distinctive.
The closing prayer asks God not to lay on people a burden like the one laid on those before and asks for pardon and mercy; it gives a direct supplication for the load the section says God removes.

In the fasting rule, God intends ease and does not intend hardship; this concrete rule parallels the section’s law of ease amid difficulty and states the same ease-versus-hardship boundary in another setting.

After setting out ablution and purification, this ayah says God does not intend difficulty but intends purification and completion of favor; it ties relief from difficulty to a divine gift as the section does.

The ayah says God wishes to lighten for people because the human was created weak; that is a specific divine easing of human constraint, supporting the section’s broadening of relief beyond one personal load.

God expands the breast of one He guides toward Islam and makes another’s breast constricted; the source-section root sh-r-ḥ is therefore given a clear direction and boundary, expansion toward guidance rather than any destination.

This ayah joins a breast expanded by God to Islam with light from its Lord, then contrasts it with hearts hardened against God’s remembrance; it brings the section’s opening chest, divine light, and raised remembrance together.

The passage contrasts a heart secure in faith with those who “شرحوا بالكفر صدرا”; the source-section root sh-r-ḥ thus also names a breast opened toward disbelief, the contrary direction to its final desire for God.
God sends tranquility into the believers’ hearts; this gives a direct Qur’anic scene of inward calm bestowed by God, matching the source section’s gloss of opened breast as light and tranquility.
This ayah says hearts find tranquility in remembrance of God; it links the section’s opened, settled chest to dhikr, adding an explicit account of how remembrance calms the heart.
A group receives the Scripture and then casts it behind their backs; the section explicitly recalls this scene as the opposite of a name raised above the back and kept in memory.
A group given the Book casts it behind its backs as if they did not know; this repeated Qur’anic scene sharpens the section’s reversal from burdened or forgetful back to an elevated, remembered name.

The one who turns away from God’s remembrance bears a burden on Resurrection Day; it is the section’s exact reverse, where turning from dhikr is joined to load-bearing rather than load-removal and elevated mention.
God grants Abraham’s descendants mercy and “لسان صدق عليا,” a high, truthful renown; this is a concrete instance of the source-section’s remembrance as honor raised to a high place.
Abraham asks God to make for him a truthful mention among later generations; the prayer gives a direct counterpart to the section’s claim that God raises the addressee’s remembrance.
The people are told that a Book has come containing “ذكركم”; the source-section root dh-k-r includes honor and mention, and this ayah makes remembrance a defining address to a whole people.
The Revelation is called a remembrance for the Prophet and his people, who will be questioned about it; this specific communal address relates to the section’s remembrance raised for its addressee.
“اذكروني أذكركم” gives reciprocal remembrance between people and God; it adds a direct relationship to the section’s image of a name raised and held in remembrance.
The command to remember the Lord inwardly and “دون الجهر من القول” (without loud speech) engages the source-section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as sound while specifying a quieter mode.

God permits houses “أن ترفع ويذكر فيها اسمه”; this ayah directly joins raising a structure to remembrance of His name, meeting the section’s linked ideas of building, elevation, and a name kept present.

The next ayah says commerce and sale do not distract these people from remembering God and establishing prayer; it contributes workers who keep their direction through worldly tasks, the section’s final labor-and-desire scene.

Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House while praying for acceptance; the source-section root r-f-ʿ links this literal construction and elevation to the section’s raising of remembrance.
God and His angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to bless and greet him; this is a concrete act of honoring the addressee, related to the section’s elevated remembrance.
Believers are told to support and honor the Messenger and glorify God morning and evening; it supplies a concrete form of public honor alongside the section’s raised name.
The human is “كادح إلى ربك كدحا,” laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him; this directly joins the section’s wearied, Godward effort to its final orientation toward God.

After Moses and his companion continue their journey to meet the servant they seek, Moses says they have met “نصبا,” fatigue; this shares the source-section root n-ṣ-b and its purposeful labor, while its context makes the exertion a journey of seeking.

The faces described as “عاملة ناصبة” are laboring and exhausted, but the surrounding passage gives them a severe punishment; the shared source-section root n-ṣ-b marks a boundary that exertion alone does not establish the right Godward direction.
88:3 supplies the weary labor, and this next ayah adds “تسقى من عين آنية,” a drink from a boiling spring; this row completes the punishment that contrasts with the section’s Lord-directed effort.

In a passage about accounting and striving, the ayah states that no bearer of a burden bears another’s burden; it gives the boundary that the section’s contrast between Moses’ requested helper and God’s direct removal makes visible.

After 53:38 states that one does not carry another’s burden, this ayah says a person has only what he strives for; its own contribution is the shift from load-bearing to personal effort, as in the section’s command after the burden is removed.

Following 53:39’s statement of personal striving, this ayah says the striving will be seen; it adds the disclosure of directed effort to the section’s rise from hidden burden to publicly raised remembrance.
After 53:39–40 describe effort and its being seen, this ayah says it will then be repaid fully; it completes the passage’s account of the consequence of one’s own labor.
A heavily burdened soul cannot have another carry its burden even if the other is a close relative; this gives a literalized boundary on human load-sharing beside the section’s burden removed by God.
Those who mislead are said to bear their own burdens and additional burdens; this is a contrary load-sharing case that clarifies the moral weight attached to the source-section’s root w-z-r.

Believers are commanded to leave trade when called to Friday prayer and hasten to God’s remembrance; this is a concrete redirection from finished worldly work toward worship, preparing the action sequence in the next ayah.

After prayer is concluded, believers disperse to seek God’s bounty and remember Him much; this ayah contributes the specific post-task movement that parallels the section’s “when free, rise and turn desire to your Lord.”

After prayer, believers are commanded to remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides; this connects the section’s upright posture and continued remembrance to a concrete worship sequence after an activity.
The command to stand before God devoutly gives a direct posture of standing in worship, a possible specific counterpart to the section’s word nasb as raising oneself upright.
The Prophet is told to remember his Lord’s name and devote himself wholly to Him; this joins the section’s raised-name motif to its final deliberate turn toward God.

After completing the rites, people are commanded to remember God; this is a direct finish-then-remembrance sequence corresponding to the section’s transition from completing work to rising for another directed act.

After 2:200’s post-rites remembrance, this ayah records the prayer “ربنا آتنا في الدنيا حسنة وفي الآخرة حسنة”; its own contribution is a desire directed to the Lord that includes both worldly and lasting good.
Following the two prayers in 2:201, this ayah says each has a share of what they earned; it completes the link between directed desire and the worker’s eventual portion.
This ayah describes one who desires the immediate life and is given some of it; it concretely supplies the worldly direction the section says an opened chest could take.

By contrast with 17:18, this ayah describes one who desires the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer; that specific desire-plus-effort pattern matches the section’s command to work and direct longing to God.
The one who transgressed and “آثر الحياة الدنيا” preferred worldly life; this is a direct opposite to the section’s final Godward desire.

79:37 names preference for worldly life, and this ayah says Hell is its shelter; its own contribution is the destination that makes the preference a consequential reversal of the section’s turning to God.
This ayah describes one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains the self from desire; it directly joins standing, the Lord, and renouncing a competing desire.
After 79:40 describes restraint out of fear of the Lord, this ayah says the Garden is the shelter; its own contribution is the outcome of that Godward orientation.
People are said to prefer the nearer life; this is the precise worldly preference that the section names as a possible direction for the opened chest.
87:16 supplies preference for nearer life, and this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more lasting; it contributes the boundary that supports the section’s final orientation to God.
The command is to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting one’s worldly share; this gives a specific balance between worldly provision and the ultimate direction toward God.
The righteous person gives wealth to purify himself; this concrete emptying of what one has contributes a material image of release before the section’s turn toward the Lord.
After 92:18 describes giving, this ayah says it is not repayment for a favor received; its own contribution removes an earthly payback motive from the act.
After 92:19 rules out repayment, this ayah says the giving seeks only the face of the Most High Lord; it directly specifies the Godward aim the section’s last ayah commands.
Following the act and its aim in 92:18–20, this ayah promises that the giver will be satisfied; it completes the relation between directed effort and its outcome.

The source-section root f-r-gh in “فرغت إلى” is glossed as deliberately turning to an undertaking; 28:10 instead says Moses’ mother’s heart became “فارغا” after she placed him in the river. The shared root and emptied-heart image are specific, though this is a different sense and a fearful scene rather than purposeful work.

God says “سنفرغ لكم” to the two weighty beings; the source-section root f-r-gh is glossed as turning deliberately to a matter, and this distinct divine use likewise presents a directed engagement, though the wording and scene differ.

The ayah asks who would turn away “عن ملة إبراهيم”; the source-section root r-gh-b names desire toward the Lord, so this opposed preposition and direction make a direct boundary around the section’s final “إلى ربك فارغب.”

2:130 asks who turns away from Abraham’s way, and this next ayah answers with Abraham’s “أسلمت لرب العالمين”; its own contribution is an explicit submission to the Lord that completes the opposite direction to turning away.
The prophets are described as hastening in good deeds and calling upon God “رغبا ورهبا”; this uses the source-section root r-gh-b for desire in a specifically God-directed supplication.
The command “ففروا إلى الله” directs people to flee toward God; it gives another explicit movement of orientation toward Him, like the section’s final turn of desire.

People aboard ships call to God sincerely when a storm strikes, promise gratitude if saved, then commit wrong after rescue; this is a sea-and-relief reversal of the section’s response of turning to the Lord after help.

At sea, people call only upon God in distress, then turn away when He saves them to land; this directly reverses the section’s Godward return after removal of a burden and also continues the mount-and-travel scene.
Those boarding a ship invoke God sincerely in danger, but associate others once safely on land; this gives a clear contrary response to the section’s final desire toward the benefactor after relief.

People in shipboard waves call God sincerely, but after rescue some remain moderate and others reject; the ayah supplies a divided response after relief that sharpens the section’s chosen Godward turn.

When hardship touches people they call their Lord, but after He lets them taste mercy some associate others with Him; this is an explicit reversal of the section’s steady desire toward the Lord after help.
A person calls the Lord in hardship with turning devotion, then forgets Him when granted favor; this directly marks the failure that the section’s final turn after relief answers.
When God bestows favor on a person, he turns away and withdraws; this states the opposite of the section’s person whose removed burden leads him back to his benefactor.
The person who receives favor turns away and draws aside, while he prays at length when harm touches him; this is a second direct reversal of the section’s post-relief orientation.
God says He left Noah’s mention among later generations; this is a concrete instance of remembrance preserved beyond the immediate scene, paralleling the raised name in the section.
37:78 preserves Noah’s mention among later generations, and this ayah adds “سلام على نوح في العالمين”; its own contribution is the honor attached to that enduring mention.
God says He left Abraham’s mention among later generations; it repeats the concrete preservation of a person’s name that the section calls raised remembrance.
37:108 says Abraham’s mention remains among later generations, and this ayah adds “سلام على إبراهيم”; its own contribution is the honor that gives that enduring mention its tone.
God says He left Moses and Aaron’s mention among later generations; this is another specific case of their remembrance being preserved beyond their own time.
37:119 preserves Moses and Aaron’s mention among later generations, and this ayah adds “سلام على موسى وهارون”; it contributes the honor joined to their lasting mention.
God says He left Elias’s mention among later generations; this repeated formulation directly parallels the section’s image of a name raised and remembered.
37:129 preserves Elias’s mention among later generations, and this ayah adds “سلام على إل ياسين”; its own contribution is the honor attached to that lasting remembrance.
In the Garden of settlement, the people say no fatigue or weariness touches them; this provides a contrary boundary to the section’s tiring work here, with relief from exertion as an eventual state.
